title: "The methods and the evidence"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110, out.width = "100%")
library(lactater)
library(dplyr)
library(gt)
plex <- requireNamespace("systemfonts", quietly = TRUE) &&
  isTRUE(suppressMessages(systemfonts::require_font("IBM Plex Sans", fallback = "sans")))
if (plex) options(lactater.font = "IBM Plex Sans")
```

lactater estimates the lactate threshold concepts that are most used in sport science. This article says how each
one is defined, how lactater computes it, what the evidence says about it, and how to collect data that does the
methods justice. Every statement points to its source, and every source links to the paper.

## Two thresholds, many methods

Most authors describe the lactate response to a step test with two thresholds and three phases: a first rise of
lactate above resting values (LT1) and a second, abrupt increase (LT2), which split the intensities into three
zones with distinct metabolic, hormonal and cardio-respiratory responses ([Hofmann & Tschakert, 2017](https://doi.org/10.3389/fphys.2017.00337)). With gas exchange,
the two boundaries can also be estimated without blood, as the estimated lactate threshold and the respiratory
compensation point: [Keir et al. (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-021-01581-z) explain the physiology behind them and how to find them, and introduce an
online app to practice on real data. The methods in
lactater fall into the three families of a review that counted 25 lactate threshold concepts: fixed lactate
concentrations, a first rise above baseline, and concepts aimed at the maximal lactate steady state (MLSS) or a
distinct change in the curve ([Faude et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)). Some still carry the name "anaerobic threshold", which is
historical: blood lactate rises because glycolysis speeds up and lactate appears faster than it is removed, not
mainly because the muscle runs short of oxygen ([Poole et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1113/JP279963)).

## How lactater computes them

The plots below are `demo_data`, a cycling test of 7 stages, with `autoplot(results, method = ...)`.

```{r methods-results}
results <- lactate_threshold(demo_data, intensity, lactate, heart_rate, plot = FALSE)
```

### Fitted curves

The 3rd and 4th degree polynomials are fitted by least squares. "B-spline" is a natural cubic
regression spline with 4 degrees of freedom. The exponential plus constant, `a + b * exp(c * x)`, is fitted by
searching `c` only, and only positive values as in [Hughson et al. (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1152/jappl.1987.62.5.1975): for a fixed `c` the model is linear in `a`
and `b`. This needs no starting values and cannot fail to converge. `lactate_fit_quality()` compares the curves on your data.

### Fixed concentrations (OBLA, Bsln+, IAT)

The intensity is found by solving the fitted curve for the target
lactate. When the curve crosses the target more than once (an early lactate dip), the last crossing where lactate rises
through it is used: from there on, lactate stays above the target.
Bsln+ takes the resting sample as the baseline, or the first stage when there is no resting sample.

```{r bsln-plus}
autoplot(results, method = "Bsln + 0.5")
```

IAT rises from the lowest lactate / intensity ratio (LT<sub>ratio</sub>) instead of from the baseline:

```{r iat}
autoplot(results, method = "IAT")
```

A fixed concentration assumes that everyone's MLSS sits at the same lactate, and it does not. In national and
international athletes the lactate at the MLSS was 3.1 +/- 0.5 mmol/L in rowing, 5.4 +/- 1.0 in cycling and 6.6 +/- 0.9
in speed skating, although the MLSS sat at 72 to 78% of the maximal workload in all three ([Beneke & von Duvillard,
1996](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199602000-00013)). In 33 men cycling it was 4.9 +/- 1.4 mmol/L, whatever their performance ([Beneke et al.,
2000](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-200006000-00016)), and in 57 men it ranged from 2.2 to 9.2 mmol/L ([Hauser et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0033-1353176)).

### The D<sub>max</sub> family

Every variant takes the point where the fitted curve lies furthest *below* a straight line that
ends at the last stage. Where the line's ends sit differs between papers, and lactater follows each one by default
(`dmax_anchor = "original"`):

* D<sub>max</sub> and Exp-D<sub>max</sub>: on the curve, "the two end points of the curve" ([Cheng et al., 1992](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2007-1021309); [Jamnick et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794)).
* ModD<sub>max</sub>: at the measured values, "the LT and the final lactate point" ([Bishop et al., 1998](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199808000-00014)).
* Log-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub> and Log-Exp-ModD<sub>max</sub>: from the Log-log threshold on the curve to "the final lactate point"
  ([Jamnick et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794)).

Other authors drew D<sub>max</sub> from the measured points too: "the two end data points" ([Bishop et al., 1998](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199808000-00014)), "the first
and last lactate measurements" ([Bentley et al., 2007](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200737070-00002)) or "the first and last measured points" ([Heuberger et al.,
2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846)). `dmax_anchor = "fitted"` puts every end on the curve and `"observed"` every end at the measured values. On a
smooth curve the choice moves D<sub>max</sub> by less than 1 W; when lactate levels off in the last stage it can move a
threshold by tens of watts.

The ModD<sub>max</sub> first rise is "at least 0.4 mmol/L" between two stages ([Heuberger et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846)); [Bishop et al. (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199808000-00014)
and [Jamnick et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794) wrote "> 0.4", which differs only when two stages differ by exactly 0.4 mmol/L. Bishop et
al. measured plasma lactate from the fingertip. Change the rise with `moddmax_rise`, for example for sweat lactate.
The resting sample is never used, and the Log-log start of the Log-*-ModD<sub>max</sub> variants is computed without it.

```{r log-poly-moddmax}
autoplot(results, method = "Log-Poly-ModDmax")
```

### Log-log

[Beaver et al. (1985)](https://doi.org/10.1152/jappl.1985.59.6.1936) split the log-log data into two segments that share the stage between them, fitted
a straight line to each, and took the threshold where the two lines cross. They chose the split by eye; [Jamnick et
al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794) took "the intersection point of the two lines with the lowest residuals sum of squares". lactater tries
every stage as the split, with at least three stages per line (a line through two points has no residuals, which
would favor the shortest segments), so Log-log needs at least five stages. When the two lines cross outside the
measured stages, the result is `NA`.

```{r log-log}
autoplot(results, method = "Log-log")
```

### LTP

[Hofmann et al. (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199706000-00005) and [Pokan et al. (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199708000-00009) found each turn point as the crossing of two regression lines
"with minimal standard deviation", inside a window: LTP1 from the first lactate value up to 4 mmol/L ([Hofmann et
al., 1997](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199706000-00005)) or 75% of the maximal power ([Pokan et al., 1997](https://doi.org/10.1097/00005768-199708000-00009)), and LTP2 from LTP1 to the maximal power. Their tests had 1-min and 90-s stages,
so the windows held many samples. With the 6 to 10 stages of a typical step test the windows hold too few stages, so
lactater fits three connected straight segments to all stages at once, trying every pair of breakpoints with at
least two stages per segment. The result is the global optimum and never depends on starting values.
`ltp_fix_first_slope = TRUE` keeps the segment before LTP1 flat.

```{r ltp}
autoplot(results, method = "LTP1")
```

### Stegmann

[Stegmann et al. (1981)](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-2008-1034604) followed blood lactate over time, during the test and in recovery (at 1, 2, 5
and 10 min). After the test lactate first rises and then falls; from the point where it is back at its end-of-exercise
value, they drew a tangent to the lactate curve of the test. The point of contact is the threshold, and the slope of
the tangent the maximal rate of lactate elimination. Give lactater the recovery samples as `recovery` (minutes and
lactate) and the stage duration as `stage_duration`: lactater puts the recovery minutes on the intensity axis at the
rate the test rose, finds the return to the end-of-exercise value by linear interpolation between the recovery
samples, and draws the tangent that touches the fitted curve from below. Some of the model's assumptions about lactate
kinetics "have been challenged" ([Faude et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)). Nor can the threshold always be found: when lactate falls fast after
the test, it is already below its end-of-exercise value at the first recovery sample, which ruled the method out in 5
of 12 elite cyclists ([Płoszczyca et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-020-00219-3)) and 6 of 57 men ([Hauser et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0033-1353176)). lactater then returns `NA`.

Here with `demo_data` (3-min stages) and recovery samples simulated for the example:

```{r stegmann}
recovery <- tibble(time = c(1, 3, 5, 7, 10), lactate = c(9.3, 9.6, 9.0, 8.2, 7.1))
stegmann <- lactate_threshold(
  demo_data, intensity, lactate, heart_rate,
  method = "Stegmann", recovery = recovery, stage_duration = 3, plot = FALSE
)
autoplot(stegmann, method = "Stegmann")
```

### Heart rate

The heart rate at each threshold is interpolated between the measured stages.

## What the evidence says

The strongest evidence on validity comes from studies that compare a threshold with the MLSS measured directly.

```{r evidence-table, echo = FALSE}
tribble(
  ~source, ~who, ~found, ~strength,
  "[Jamnick et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199794)",
  "17 trained male cyclists; five step tests (1, 3, 4, 7 and 10-min stages) and constant-power bouts to find their
  MLSS; venous blood",
  "Log-Poly-ModD<sub>max</sub> from the 4-min test gave the best estimate of the MLSS (mean difference 1.1 W, ICC
  0.96). D<sub>max</sub> differed from the MLSS by 19 to 49 W, and OBLA 4.0 overestimated it in every test.",
  "Single study",
  "[P\u0142oszczyca et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13102-020-00219-3)",
  "12 elite male cyclists (V&#775;O<sub>2max</sub> 71 mL/kg/min); 3-min stages of +40 W and 30-min constant-power bouts;
  fingertip blood, Biosen",
  "D<sub>max</sub> was 1.7 +/- 3.9 W below the MLSS, and Stegmann's IAT 4.3 +/- 7.9 W below in the 7 riders it could be
  computed for. Bsln + 1.0 was 6.7 W below on average but far off in single riders. ModD<sub>max</sub> and OBLA 4.0
  overestimated the MLSS by 32 and 43 W.",
  "Single study",
  "[Hauser et al., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1055/s-0033-1353176)",
  "57 men from untrained to 14 h of training a week; 4-min stages of +40 W and 30-min constant-power bouts; earlobe
  blood, Biosen",
  "OBLA 4.0 was 7.4 +/- 25.1 W below the MLSS and Stegmann's IAT 12.4 +/- 24.6 W above it; LT<sub>ratio</sub> + 1.5 mmol/L,
  the IAT of lactater, was 37.4 +/- 26.4 W below. Despite correlations of 0.83 to 0.89, single athletes were far off.",
  "Single study",
  "[Heuberger et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0206846)",
  "48 male cyclists, 109 tests (24 on placebo); five tests each; venous blood, Lactate Pro 2",
  "Intra-subject variation over five tests: 3.4% for D<sub>max</sub>, 3.6% for IAT, 3.8% for 4 mmol/L, 4.3% for
  ModD<sub>max</sub>. ModD<sub>max</sub> predicted a time trial best (r = 0.94); 4 mmol/L was a simpler
  alternative.",
  "Single study",
  "[Jamnick et al., 2020](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-020-01322-8)",
  "Review of the methods to determine exercise intensity",
  "LT1 has some evidence for separating the moderate and heavy domains; most methods have little for the heavy and
  severe domains. Test-retest variation: D<sub>max</sub> 3.8-10.3%, OBLA 4.0 3.1-8.2%, Bsln+ 0.5, 1.0 and 1.5
  1.2-3.7%, 3.4-12.6% and 3.1-3.4%. One athlete's threshold can differ by about 30% between methods. Bsln+ 1.5
  estimated the MLSS in two studies with 3-min stages, not with other stage lengths.",
  "Review"
) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_markdown(columns = everything()) |>
  cols_label(source = "Source", who = "Who and how", found = "What it found", strength = "Evidence") |>
  cols_width(source ~ pct(17), who ~ pct(27), found ~ pct(44), strength ~ pct(12)) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(v_align = "top"), cells_body()) |>
  tab_style(cell_text(color = "#5b6672"), cells_body(columns = strength)) |>
  gt_lactater()
```

How close a method lands to the MLSS depends on the protocol and the athletes: D<sub>max</sub> was within 2 W of it
with 3-min stages in elite cyclists, but 19 to 49 W off in the study of Jamnick et al. Most of this evidence comes from trained,
male, cycling populations; check how well it matches the athletes you test.

Whether the MLSS is the boundary between the heavy and the severe domains is itself debated. [Jones et al.
(2019)](https://doi.org/10.14814/phy2.14098) argue that the MLSS, as usually measured, falls below the maximal metabolic steady state, and that the critical
power marks the boundary. In a meta-analysis of 10 studies the critical power was 12 W above the MLSS on average, with
95% limits of agreement from -19 to 44 W, and further above it in fitter and younger people ([Micheli et al.,
2025](https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.19060)).

### Check it in your own athletes

Constant-load bouts give the MLSS itself. `lactate_mlss()` finds it and how far each threshold of the step test lies
from it, and [Beyond the step test](beyond-the-step-test.html#the-maximal-lactate-steady-state-mlss) explains how to run
the bouts and what the studies comparing the MLSS with the critical power found.

## Collecting good data

The methods are only as good as the test behind them: stage duration, sampling site, sample type and analyzer
all change the numbers. [Best practices for a step test](best-practices.html) collects what the literature says,
as a checklist for running a test and analyzing it.

## Methods lactater does not include

Keul's and Simon's thresholds are the points where the curve's tangent reaches 51 and 45 degrees ([Faude et al.,
2009](https://doi.org/10.2165/00007256-200939060-00003)). An angle depends on how the axes are scaled, which only the original papers define, so they wait
for those papers.
